categories.name: Organization design and roles
categories.summary: Who does what, who decides, and who covers when someone is out. In a small practice a few people hold many roles, so the risk is not confusion but a function that stops when one person is away.
good_looks_like: A one-page chart shows every function, the person responsible and a named backup.
Each role has a short written list of duties and the decisions it may make alone.
Work done by vendors or software has a named person who checks it.
The chart is reviewed whenever someone joins, leaves or a vendor changes.
failure_modes: Only one person knows how payroll, credentialing or the billing system works, and that person leaves.
The owner does tasks a staff member could do, at ten times the cost.
Two people each assume the other is following up denials or renewals.
A vendor's work is never checked because nobody owns the relationship.
key_questions: Could each critical function run for two weeks without its usual person?
Which tasks does the owner do that someone else could?
Who checks the work of each vendor and each automated process?
When was the list of roles last updated?

actions.detail: List functions down the page: clinical, scheduling or census, billing, credentialing, finance, compliance, technology. Add owner and backup.
The backup performs the task at least once a quarter with the written procedure.
Each quarter, hand one recurring task to staff, a vendor or software, with a check.

actions.action: Name an owner for every vendor
actions.detail: One person receives the vendor's reports and reviews performance.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. In practices with fewer than five people the chart is mostly about backups. Where billing is run by a vendor or by software agents, the role that matters is the person who oversees them.
categories.evidence_note: Standard management practice, reflected in the MGMA body of knowledge and the Baldrige workforce criteria. No measured benchmark applies.

metrics.name: Critical functions with a trained backup
metrics.definition: Share of the practice's critical functions for which a second person has the access, the written procedure and recent practice to perform it.
metrics.formula: Functions with a backup who performed the task in the last 6 months / critical functions
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100% for payroll, billing submission, credentialing and bank access.
metrics.data_hint: The function chart, reviewed each quarter.

categories.name: Hiring and onboarding
categories.summary: Finding, choosing and starting clinicians and staff. For clinicians the hidden constraint is time: payer enrollment takes months, and a new clinician produces little revenue until it is done.
good_looks_like: Each opening has a written role, pay range and the three things the person must be able to do.
Clinician enrollment with Medicare, Medicaid and the main plans starts the day the offer is signed.
New hires get a written first-90-day plan and a named person to ask.
A new clinician's first 20 charts are reviewed for coding and documentation.
failure_modes: A clinician starts seeing patients before enrollment is effective, and those visits cannot be billed.
Hiring happens only after someone quits, so the practice runs short for months.
A new biller learns from the last biller's habits, including the wrong ones.
References and license or exclusion checks are skipped for a familiar candidate.
key_questions: How long did our last hire take from posting to start, and from start to full productivity?
For our last clinician, how many days passed between start date and the first payable visit for each payer?
Do we check licenses, references and exclusion lists before every offer?
Is there a written plan for a new person's first 90 days?

actions.detail: Collect the documents with the signed offer. File Medicare, Medicaid and plan applications that week, and track each one weekly.
Verify license and board status, check federal and state exclusion lists, and call references.
Systems access, training, shadowing, first tasks, and check-ins at 30, 60 and 90 days.

actions.action: Audit a new clinician's first charts
actions.detail: Review 20 notes in the first month for level, documentation and place of service.

categories.applies_when: Any practice that hires. Enrollment lead time is the main issue for clinicians. Medicare processes most clean online applications within 15 to 50 days, and each health plan adds its own timeline.
categories.evidence_note: Medicare processing times are published by the contractor. Plan credentialing timelines vary by contract and are not published. Hiring practices are professional guidance.

metrics.name: Days to fill an open position
metrics.definition: Calendar days from the decision to hire to the person's first day.
metrics.formula: Start date - date the opening was approved
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. For clinicians, track days from start date to the first payable visit for each payer as well.

metrics.name: New hires still employed after 12 months
metrics.definition: Share of people hired in a period who are still with the practice one year after their start date.
metrics.formula: Hires still employed at 12 months / hires in the period
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. In a small practice count people, not percentages: each early departure is worth a review.

categories.name: Clinician compensation design
categories.summary: How physicians and advanced practice clinicians are paid: salary, productivity, quality incentives, and pay for call or directorships. The plan should be affordable, legal, and reward what the practice needs.
good_looks_like: The plan fits on one page and each clinician can calculate their own pay.
Total pay is compared each year with a named survey for the specialty.
Productivity is measured in work relative value units, which do not change with payer mix.
Any incentive is tied to personally performed work or to quality, never to referrals for services the practice profits from.
failure_modes: Pay tied to collections punishes clinicians for the payer mix and for billing office errors.
A productivity plan with no audit rewards higher visit levels, and levels drift upward.
Guaranteed salaries exceed what the clinician's work brings in, and nobody has done the arithmetic.
Bonuses that vary with ancillary or facility referrals create exposure under the self-referral law.
key_questions: What does each clinician cost in total, and what do they collect?
How does each clinician's pay per work unit compare with the survey median?
Does any part of pay depend on referrals or on services the clinician does not personally perform?
Is every clinician's level mix audited at least yearly?

actions.action: Calculate cost and collections per clinician
actions.detail: Total pay with taxes and benefits against collections attributable to that clinician, each year.
Compare with a named survey median for specialty and region, and record the source.

actions.action: Pair productivity pay with a coding audit
actions.detail: Any plan that pays more for more work units needs an independent audit of levels.
Bonuses and directorship pay must fit the self-referral and kickback rules.

categories.applies_when: Any practice with more than one clinician, and solo owners deciding their own salary. Nurse practitioners and physician assistants are paid by Medicare at 85% of the physician rate, which changes their break-even volume.
categories.evidence_note: Survey medians are measured but come mostly from large groups. The self-referral limits on compensation are federal regulation. Plan design itself is judgment.

metrics.name: Compensation per work RVU
metrics.definition: Total cash compensation for a clinician divided by the work relative value units of the services that clinician personally performed.
metrics.formula: Total compensation / work RVUs personally performed
metrics.benchmark_typical: about $53 family medicine, $56 internal medicine, $34 primary care nurse practitioner
metrics.benchmark_note: AMGA medians, 2025 data, from 451 mostly large groups. Use as a reference point, not a target. A figure far below the median can mean unusually high billed work units.
metrics.data_hint: Payroll for pay. The billing system for services by rendering clinician, multiplied by the Medicare work value of each code.

metrics.name: Clinician compensation as a share of collections
metrics.definition: Total pay and benefits of all clinicians, including a market wage for owners, as a share of professional collections.
metrics.formula: Clinician pay, taxes and benefits / professional collections
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The useful comparison is with what is left: support cost plus clinician cost should leave a margin.

categories.name: Staff pay and incentives
categories.summary: Pay, raises, benefits and bonuses for non-clinician staff. Wages for front office and clinical support roles have risen faster than physician payment, so pay must be checked against the local market each year.
good_looks_like: Each role has a pay range based on local market data, reviewed yearly.
Raises follow a stated rule tied to performance and market movement.
Any bonus rewards accurate, complete work, such as clean claims or days in receivables, not raw billing volume.
Benefits are priced and communicated as part of total pay.
failure_modes: The best employee leaves for two dollars an hour more because nobody checked the market.
A bonus on charges or claims submitted rewards speed over accuracy.
Long-serving staff are paid less than new hires for the same job.
Overtime is paid routinely because the workload was never matched to staffing.
key_questions: When did we last compare each role's pay with local wages?
Is any staff bonus tied to dollars billed?
What would it cost to replace our most important staff member?
How much overtime did we pay last quarter?

actions.action: Check pay against the market yearly
actions.detail: Use a published survey or local job postings for each role, and record what you found.

actions.action: Tie incentives to quality of work
actions.detail: Use accuracy and timeliness measures. Never pay billing staff a share of charges.
Persistent overtime is a staffing or process problem.

categories.applies_when: Practices with employed staff. Practices that outsource billing or use automation have fewer roles but depend more on each one.
categories.evidence_note: MGMA publishes staff pay data, mostly behind a paywall. The figures cited are from its free reports. Incentive design is professional guidance.

metrics.name: Staff pay against the local market
metrics.definition: Each role's pay rate as a percentage of the local market median for that role.
metrics.formula: Role pay rate / local market median for the role
metrics.benchmark_note: A reasonable band, not a published standard. MGMA reports five-year pay growth to 2025 of 22.0% for medical receptionists and 20.6% for medical assistants, so old pay ranges are likely stale.
metrics.data_hint: Payroll, compared with a wage survey or current local postings.

categories.name: Productivity, accountability and performance
categories.summary: Clear expectations for each role, a regular look at whether they are met, and a conversation when they are not. For automated work, the same idea applies: a standard, a log and a review.
good_looks_like: Each role has two or three measurable standards, such as claims worked per day or denials touched within 48 hours.
Work queues show what is waiting and how old it is, every day.
Every person has a written review at least once a year.
Automated processes have a run log and a monthly human sample.
failure_modes: Nobody notices a queue growing until receivables have aged by a month.
Performance problems are discussed for the first time at termination.
Activity is measured, such as calls made, while results are not.
Software runs unattended and its errors are found by a payer.
key_questions: What are the two measures that tell us each role is being done well?
How old is the oldest item in each work queue today?
Has every person had a written review in the last 12 months?
Who reviews what our automated processes did last month?

actions.action: Set two or three standards per role
actions.detail: Choose measures of results the person controls, and review them monthly.
Oldest item and count for charges, rejections, denials, unposted payments and credentialing.
Once a year at minimum, with a short quarterly check-in.
Review a fixed number of automated actions each month against the source record.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. With in-house billing staff the measures are per person. With a billing company, they become contract service levels. With software agents, they are run logs and a sampled review.
categories.evidence_note: Management practice. The few measured productivity figures, such as coding encounters per day, come from MGMA and vary widely with role definitions.

metrics.name: Staff with a performance review in the last 12 months
metrics.definition: Share of employees who have had a written review within the past year.
metrics.formula: Employees reviewed in the last 12 months / employees
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is everyone.

metrics.name: Claims or accounts worked per billing full-time equivalent
metrics.definition: Output of billing staff per full-time person, in claims submitted, accounts followed up or encounters coded per day.
metrics.formula: Units of work completed / full-time equivalents / working days
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA reported coding staff handling 41 encounters a day in 2022, down from 75 in 2019. Definitions differ so much that only your own trend is comparable.
metrics.data_hint: Billing system productivity reports by user.

categories.name: Training and competency
categories.summary: What each person must know to do the job correctly, taught at hire and refreshed every year. Coding and payer rules change annually, and clinicians choose most codes themselves.
good_looks_like: New staff and clinicians are trained on the systems, privacy rules and the practice's billing rules before working alone.
Clinicians receive coding education each year, built from their own audit results.
Annual code and fee schedule changes are reviewed every December.
Training is recorded: who, what, when.
failure_modes: Clinicians last learned visit coding in residency, before the rules changed.
A code is deleted on January 1 and the practice keeps billing it for weeks.
Privacy training was done once at hire and never again.
There is no record of training when an auditor asks for it.
key_questions: When did each clinician last receive coding education specific to our visit types?
Who reviews the annual code and Medicare payment changes for us?
Can we show a record of privacy and compliance training for everyone?
Does anyone on the team, or an outside reviewer, hold a coding certification?

actions.detail: After each chart audit, a one-hour session on the patterns found, for all clinicians.
New, deleted and revised codes and the Medicare final rule, turned into a one-page summary.
Date, topic, attendees and materials, kept with the compliance files.
Each backup performs the task quarterly.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. Where billing is outsourced or automated, the clinicians still choose the codes and need the training, and someone inside the practice must understand enough to supervise.
categories.evidence_note: Federal compliance guidance lists training as one of seven program elements and expects it at hire and periodically. Hours and content are left to the practice.

metrics.name: Training hours per person per year
metrics.definition: Recorded hours of job, coding, privacy and compliance training for each clinician and staff member in a year.
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. A practical floor is one hour of compliance and privacy training and one coding session for every clinician each year.

categories.name: Retention, culture and well-being
categories.summary: Keeping the people the practice depends on, and noticing overload before it becomes a resignation. Replacing a clinician costs months of lost revenue, and burnout is common among physicians.
good_looks_like: Turnover is counted each year by role, and every departure has an exit conversation.
Workload is looked at directly: visits per day, after-hours charting, calls.
Clinicians have protected time off with real coverage.
The owner's own workload and health are treated as a business risk.
failure_modes: A key person resigns and the reasons were known for a year.
The owner covers every gap personally until the owner becomes the gap.
After-hours documentation grows unnoticed.
Good work is never acknowledged, only errors.
key_questions: Who left in the last two years, and why?
How many hours a week does each clinician chart after hours?
When did each clinician, including the owner, last take a full week off?
What would make our most important person leave?

actions.action: Count turnover and hold exit conversations
actions.detail: Record role, tenure and reason for every departure.

actions.action: Ask about workload twice a year
actions.detail: A short private conversation or survey on workload, after-hours work and obstacles.

actions.action: Arrange real coverage for time off
actions.detail: A written arrangement so that vacation is not followed by a backlog.

actions.action: Agree a retention plan for key people
actions.detail: For anyone whose loss would cut revenue sharply: pay review, schedule, growth path.

categories.applies_when: Every practice. In very small practices each departure is a crisis, so retention of one or two key people matters more than a turnover percentage.
categories.evidence_note: Turnover medians are measured by MGMA and burnout rates by the AMA. Both come from samples dominated by larger organizations.

metrics.name: Annual staff turnover
metrics.definition: Departures during the year as a share of average headcount, counted by role group.
metrics.benchmark_note: MGMA single-specialty medians, 2025 data. The 2022 peak was 40% for front office staff. The red flag is a judgment, not a published threshold.

metrics.name: Clinicians reporting burnout
metrics.definition: Share of clinicians who report at least one symptom of burnout on a short validated survey question.
metrics.benchmark_note: AMA, 2025 data, from a health-system sample: 41.9%, and 45% in family medicine. In a practice of a few clinicians, ask each one directly.
metrics.data_hint: A one-question annual survey or a direct conversation.

categories.name: Employment agreements and HR compliance
categories.summary: The contracts and employment rules that apply to clinicians and staff: written agreements, restrictive covenants, wage and hour law, employee or contractor status, personnel files and workplace safety.
good_looks_like: Every clinician has a signed, current agreement covering pay, duties, term, termination and malpractice tail.
Advanced practice clinicians have whatever supervision or collaboration document the state requires.
Staff are correctly classed for overtime, and contractors truly are contractors.
Personnel files hold license checks, training records and required forms.
failure_modes: A clinician works for years on an expired or unsigned agreement.
A non-compete is unenforceable as written, or enforceable against the owner in a way nobody intended.
A long-time contractor is really an employee, with back taxes and penalties.
Nobody knows who pays for malpractice tail coverage when a clinician leaves.
key_questions: Does every clinician have a signed agreement that matches how they are actually paid?
What happens to patients, records and tail coverage if a clinician leaves?
Are our advanced practice clinicians' state-required protocols signed and current?
Has anyone reviewed how we classify each worker?

actions.detail: Check pay terms, term dates, covenants and tail coverage against current practice.
Supervision or collaboration agreements, filed where the state requires.
State law decides what is enforceable and for how long.
Review each contractor against the tax and labor tests.

categories.applies_when: Every practice with clinicians or staff other than the owner. State law varies widely. In Florida, for example, an employee covenant of six months or less is presumed reasonable and one over two years presumed unreasonable.
categories.evidence_note: Covenant rules are state statute. The federal rule that would have banned most non-competes was struck down and removed in 2026. Classification and wage rules are federal and state law.

metrics.name: Clinicians and key staff with a signed, current agreement
metrics.definition: Share of clinicians and key staff whose written agreement is signed, unexpired and matches their current pay and duties.
metrics.formula: People with a current signed agreement / clinicians and key staff
metrics.benchmark_note: No reliable public benchmark was found. Compare with your own trend. The target from first principles is 100%.

categories.name: Outsourcing versus in-house
categories.summary: Whether billing, coding, credentialing, bookkeeping and technology are done by employees, by a vendor, or by software. Each model trades cost against control, and the practice stays responsible for the result in all of them.
good_looks_like: The practice knows its full cost for each function under the current model.
Any vendor contract states service levels, reporting, data ownership and how to leave.
Someone inside the practice understands the work well enough to judge it.
Results are compared before and after any change of model.
failure_modes: A percentage-of-collections vendor works the easy claims and lets the hard ones age.
The practice cannot get its own data back when it wants to leave.
Work is brought in-house or automated to save money, and nobody is left who can check it.
The owner believes responsibility for claims moved to the vendor. It did not.
key_questions: What does each function cost us now, as a share of collections?
What do our vendor contracts say about data, reporting and termination?
Who inside the practice reviews the vendor's or the software's work?
What happened to net collections and receivables after our last change?

actions.action: Calculate the full cost of each model
actions.detail: Include staff time, software, clearinghouse fees and the owner's oversight time.

actions.action: Put service levels in the contract
actions.detail: Days to submit, denial follow-up time, reporting, data return on exit.
An outside coding audit and a monthly look at receivables and denials, whatever the model.

actions.action: Measure before and after any change
actions.detail: Net collection rate, days in receivables and denial rate for six months each side.

categories.applies_when: Every practice makes this choice for billing and usually for bookkeeping, payroll and technology. Very small practices often outsource. Practices that automate with software agents face the same questions with a different vendor.
categories.evidence_note: Fee ranges come from an old trade article and are widely repeated without newer data. Federal compliance guidance is clear that a practice remains responsible for claims a vendor submits.

metrics.name: Outsourced billing fee as a share of collections
metrics.definition: What the practice pays a billing company, as a percentage of the collections that company handles.
metrics.formula: Billing vendor fees / collections handled by the vendor
metrics.benchmark_note: Physicians Practice, 2010: 4% to 5% for high-payment specialties, 8% to 10% for primary care. No current measured benchmark was found. Compare with your own full in-house cost.
metrics.data_hint: Vendor invoices and the income statement.
